analysis.one_liner: Lets the Federal Trade Commission penalize brand drug makers that reformulate drugs or pile up patents to block generic competition.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to stop drug makers from delaying cheaper generics cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee in June 2019 but was never brought up for a Senate vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it an unfair method of competition, enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission, when a brand-name drug maker pulls its older drug off the market or reformulates it right before a generic is set to arrive, forcing patients onto the pricier new version — a practice called product hopping. The Senate version that cleared committee would also cap, at 20, how many patents a biologic drug maker can assert in a lawsuit against a biosimilar competitor. The committee approved it with bipartisan support, but Senate leaders never scheduled it for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and payers — including employers, insurers, and government health programs — who currently keep paying brand-name prices when a manufacturer switches patients to a reformulated drug or buries generic rivals in patent litigation. Generic and biosimilar makers also gain a clearer path to market.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair method of competition under the FTC Act for a drug maker to withdraw approval of a drug, discontinue it, destroy inventory, or take steps that disadvantage it, and then sell a reformulated follow-on version, in the window around a generic or biosimilar application.
Lets the FTC impose penalties, sue to stop the conduct in federal court, and seek disgorgement of profits and restitution, with a five-year window for those claims.
Caps at 20 the number of patents a biologic maker can assert in infringement suits against biosimilar applicants, limiting a common tactic of extending monopolies through patent litigation.
Includes a safety carve-out: a manufacturer can rebut the presumption by showing it withdrew a drug for documented safety reasons or had legitimate pro-competitive reasons for the change.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose revenue from extended market exclusivity would shrink as generics and biosimilars reach the market sooner. Advocates for the industry argue that exclusivity revenue funds research and development.

drawbacks.text: The committee substitute dropped the bill's original prohibition on patent thicketing — amassing patents to delay generic entry — narrowing the bill to product hopping and a patent cap, so the patent-pileup tactic itself remained unaddressed.
The 20-patent cap in the reported bill still leaves a biologic maker a large number of patents to assert against a biosimilar applicant, and courts can raise the number for good cause.

Brand manufacturers argue that revenue from exclusivity and reformulations funds continued drug development, and enforcement relies on case-by-case FTC litigation, which takes years and cannot by itself lower prices already being paid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted antitrust remedy aimed at specific delay tactics rather than a broad price-control scheme, so its main cost falls on brand manufacturers' extended-exclusivity revenue rather than on taxpayers or consumers. Its weakness is that the Senate-reported version narrowed the original bill — dropping the patent thicketing ban — and its benefits depend on the FTC choosing to litigate case by case.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it in June 2019 and it was placed on the Senate's legislative calendar, but no senator ever brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator John Cornyn introduced the bill on May 9, 2019 with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Democrats Blumenthal, Murray, and Durbin and Republicans Capito, Scott of Florida, Kennedy, and Hawley.
The introduced version prohibited both product hopping and patent thicketing by drug manufacturers.
On June 27-28, 2019, the Senate Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and Senator Graham reported it to the Senate.

The reported version dropped the patent thicketing prohibition, retained the product hopping prohibition, and added a limit of 20 patents that biologic makers may assert against biosimilar applicants.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 132, and the record shows no further action — no floor vote, motion, or reconvened consideration — through the end of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because the tactics the bill targeted — pulling or reworking an older drug to move patients to a still-protected version, and dense patent litigation against biosimilars — remained lawful and profitable. Patients who need those drugs continued paying brand-name prices.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was a Republican and its 13 cosponsors split 5 Democrats, 7 Republicans, and 1 Independent; the Republican-run Judiciary Committee reported it favorably, so the bill itself had support from both parties, and the record does not show who opposed it.

industries.note: The bill would make product hopping an unfair method of competition and cap patent assertions against biosimilars, cutting off ways these companies extend monopolies after patents on the original drug run out. Their gain from those tactics comes directly out of what patients and health plans pay.

The bill clears obstacles these companies face — withdrawn reference drugs, inventory destruction, and multi-patent litigation — letting them bring lower-cost versions to market sooner. Their gain is the consumer's savings.

industries.industry: Insurers, employers, and government health programs as drug payers
industries.note: Earlier generic and biosimilar entry lowers drug costs for health plans and public programs like Medicare and Medicaid, reducing premiums and taxpayer spending. The record does not quantify the savings.
